Workbench Radio: Tomás Reyes on fixing old bikes (2026-11-15)
Welcome to Workbench Radio, I'm Maya Okafor. My guest today runs a community bike shop in Montreal. Thanks Maya, I'm Tomás Reyes, glad to be here. Tomás, why do so many old bikes end up in the trash? Mostly because people think a rusty chain means the bike is dead. A chain costs twenty dollars and ten minutes. The frame is the expensive part, and a steel frame from the eighties will outlive all of us. So what stops people from fixing them? Parts. Newer bikes use proprietary parts that only the brand sells, and some of them need software to adjust the gears. This episode is brought to you by Gearbox Insurance. Gearbox covers your bike against theft for five dollars a month. Visit gearbox dot example.

Workbench Radio: Tomás Reyes on fixing old bikes (2026-11-15)
This episode is brought to you by Gearbox Insurance. Gearbox covers your bike against theft for five dollars a month. Visit gearbox dot example. Back to it. Is that where the right to repair comes in? Exactly. If the manufacturer won't sell the part or share the manual, the bike becomes a disposable product. Repair laws would force them to publish manuals and sell parts for ten years. Quebec already passed a law against planned obsolescence, and I think bikes should be next. You also teach kids. What do they learn first? To fix a flat. Then to true a wheel: you spin it, watch where the rim wobbles and tighten the spokes on the other side, a quarter turn at a time. A kid who trued their own wheel never looks at a broken thing the same way again.

Workbench Radio: Tomás Reyes on fixing old bikes (2026-11-15)
A kid who trued their own wheel never looks at a broken thing the same way again. That's a great line. What's one thing listeners can do? Before you buy a new bike, take your old one to a community shop. Nine times out of ten we get it riding for under fifty dollars. Tomás Reyes, thank you. That's Workbench Radio for today.
